metaData.originalTitle: Browser Use：为 Agent 构建 Runtime Harness
metaData.title: Browser Use: Building a Runtime Harness for Agents
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article details how to build an open-source tool based on the Chrome DevTools Protocol that enables AI agents to operate real browsers for multi-dimensional verification—including visual, interactive, and console checks—thereby ensuring the delivery quality of web products.
metaData.summary: The article points out that when AI agents participate in front-end development, relying solely on static code analysis cannot guarantee the correctness of web interfaces, as many issues (such as layout overflow, asynchronous timing, and console errors) only surface at runtime. To address this, the author's team developed an open-source tool based on the Chrome DevTools Protocol, allowing agents to operate real browsers and perform verification across six dimensions: path, content, visual, interaction, console, and network. The article elaborates on the tool's design philosophy, core principle (only web page content is the single source of truth), workflow (Contract mode), real-world verification cases, and two practical approaches (Heavy QA and Fast Testing), along with cost optimization techniques. The conclusion is that runtime verification is a crucial component of the Agent Harness, and fully managed agent development is on the horizon.

mainPoints.point: AI agents must perceive the actual rendered results in the browser, not just rely on static code.
mainPoints.explanation: The correctness of a web interface results from the runtime combination of code, styles, data, container dimensions, and more, which static analysis cannot guarantee. Agents need to verify delivery quality through browser inspection, just like human developers.

mainPoints.point: The six-dimensional verification system built on CDP is a core capability.
mainPoints.explanation: Through the Chrome DevTools Protocol, agents can verify pages across six dimensions—path, content, visual, interaction, console, and network—covering almost all issues related to whether a web product 'works'.

mainPoints.point: The Contract mode is key to efficient verification, preventing agents from aimlessly consuming tokens.
mainPoints.explanation: Using structured JSON to define 'what to test', agents execute test cases one by one, recording failure experiences and timing information through progressive notes, which significantly improves the efficiency and accuracy of subsequent operations.

mainPoints.point: Balancing visual and DOM operations is central to cost optimization.
mainPoints.explanation: Screenshots are costly but suitable for layout verification, while DOM operations are cheaper but better for precise attribute reading. The best practice is to balance the two, supplemented by auxiliary methods like bordered screenshots and VET overlays to enhance detection capabilities.

keyQuotes: Correct code does not equal a correct interface. Compilation, build, and type checking can only prove that the code has no obvious engineering errors, but they cannot prove that the user won't see a blank page, that there are no console errors, or that interactive effects meet expectations.
Only web page content is the single source of truth; code is merely a reference.

Agents naturally tend to judge correctness by reading code. If an agent sees that a component's width is set to 330px, it assumes the width is 330px. However, the actual rendering is influenced by factors like the parent container's max-width, box-sizing, padding, and flex-shrink, so the final computed value may be completely different.

In the future, what an agent delivers should not just be a diff, but rather: 'I wrote the code, opened the page, walked through the path, verified the content, checked the interaction, confirmed the visuals, found no critical anomalies, and left reusable verification evidence.'

relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article details how to migrate Andrej Karpathy's AutoResearch concept to the field of software development, constructing a system capable of fully automating GitHub Issue processing through multi-AI Agent cross-review, 5-dimensional quantitative scoring, and feedback-driven iteration.

relatedArticles.title: Harness Engineering: Enabling Coding Agents to Reliably Complete Long-Horizon Tasks
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article introduces the Harness Engineering framework, which addresses the reliability challenges of Coding Agents in large-scale, long-horizon tasks through task decomposition, parallel scheduling, File-as-Progress state persistence, and multi-layered retry mechanisms.

relatedArticles.title: Understanding Hermes in One Article: How the New Top-Tier Agent Self-Evolves from Experience

relatedArticles.title: Harness Is Not the Goal, Knowledge Is the Moat — Knowledge Accumulation Practices of an AI Engineering Delivery Team

relatedArticles.title: After Reading the Claude Code Source Code, I Realized: The Differences Between Skills, MCP, and Rules Are Not as Big as You Think
